analysis.one_liner: Bans the government from ever approving genetically engineered fish for sale.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by a bipartisan group of 15 cosponsors, never got a hearing or a vote and died in a House subcommittee after the full two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite federal food law so that any genetically engineered fish is automatically considered unsafe — both as an animal drug and as adulterated food — making it illegal for the Food and Drug Administration to approve one for sale, no matter what its scientists conclude. It was introduced by Alaska's at-large Republican congressman with a mostly Democratic list of cosponsors, sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Health Subcommittee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Commercial fishing communities, especially wild-caught salmon producers in Alaska and the Pacific Northwest, would face no competition from lab-altered farmed fish. Consumers who want assurance that no genetically engineered fish reaches store shelves would get a legal guarantee, since the bill would make such fish illegal to sell rather than merely subject to FDA review.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wild-caught fishing communities and consumers wary of engineered food

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a paragraph to federal drug law declaring that 'a genetically engineered fish shall be deemed unsafe,' including as adulterated food, so the FDA could not approve one under any circumstances.
This goes beyond current law, under which the FDA already reviews genetically engineered animals through its new-animal-drug process; the bill would remove the agency's discretion entirely.

analysis.who_pays: Biotechnology companies developing genetically engineered fish would lose their entire prospective U.S. market. Consumers could pay more for fish, since a faster-growing engineered salmon that the FDA might have approved as safe would never reach the market.
analysis.who_pays_short: Biotech developers and shoppers seeking cheaper fish

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides FDA judgment by deeming genetically engineered fish unsafe 'notwithstanding any other provision' of the law, meaning a blanket legislative ban would replace the agency's scientific review process.

It would permanently block a product that could offer a cheaper, faster-growing source of salmon; in fact, the FDA later approved the AquAdvantage engineered salmon in 2015 after its own review, under general knowledge outside this bill's record.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives consumers and traditional fishing interests a hard guarantee that no engineered fish will be sold, at the cost of removing the FDA's science-based approval path entirely and foreclosing a potentially cheaper protein source. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how much weight you give the precautionary principle versus the agency's own safety review, which ultimately did approve engineered salmon. The bigger problem was process: with no hearing or vote, Congress never actually weighed these trade-offs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, then to the Health Subcommittee a week later, and sat there with no hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Young of Alaska introduced the bill on February 8, 2011, joined by Reps. Wu, Jones, DeFazio, Stark, and Polis.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and to the Subcommittee on Health on February 15, 2011.
The bill attracted 15 cosponsors — 14 Democrats and 1 Republican — but received no further action before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Biotech developers kept the ability to seek FDA approval on the agency's own timetable — the FDA went on to approve engineered salmon in 2015 — and the conventional fishing industry got no legislative shield, but also lost nothing. Consumers were left exactly where they started, with no new law and no vote ever taken.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Biotech developers and the status quo

for.name: Rep. Don Young
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it as its sole original Republican sponsor.

for.name: Reps. Wu, Jones, DeFazio, Stark, and Polis
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors on introduction day, five of the bill's eventual 15 cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never scheduled a markup or hearing, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Subcommittee on Health
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 15, 2011 and took no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Support crossed party lines from the start: a Republican sponsor from Alaska drew 14 Democratic and 1 Republican cosponsor, and the bill's problem was committee inaction, not a party split.

industries.note: The bill would have wiped out their entire U.S. market by deeming their product unsafe by law. Because the ban overrides FDA review rather than relying on it, the public would also lose access to a product the agency might have cleared as safe.

They would be protected from a new, faster-growing farmed competitor, which tends to keep fish prices higher. The sponsor represents Alaska, whose salmon fleet is the industry's main stakeholder here.
